sections.name: CHIEF_COMPLAINT
sections.heading: CHIEF COMPLAINT
sections.text:
Recurrent headaches of approximately four months duration. Patient reports

intermittent episodes of moderate-to-severe headache, predominantly unilateral,

with occasional sensitivity to light (photophobia).

sections.name: HPI
sections.heading: HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
sections.text:
Mr. Rohan Iyer, a 26-year-old male software engineer, presents to the neurology

outpatient clinic with complaints of recurrent headaches that began approximately

four months ago (around March 2024). The headaches are described as intermittent,
throbbing in character, predominantly affecting the right temporal and frontal
regions. Each episode typically lasts between 4 to 12 hours.

The patient reports associated photophobia during the more intense episodes but

denies any associated phonophobia, nausea, vomiting, or visual aura. The

headaches occur approximately two to three times per week. No identifiable
trigger has been reliably established, though the patient notes worsening with
prolonged screen exposure and sleep deprivation.

There is no history of head trauma, loss of consciousness, seizures, focal

weakness, speech disturbance, diplopia, or gait abnormality. The patient has

not experienced any recent febrile illness or neck stiffness.

Over-the-counter analgesics (Paracetamol 500 mg as needed) have provided

partial relief. The patient has not received any prior specialist evaluation

for headaches.

sections.name: FAMILY_HISTORY
sections.heading: FAMILY HISTORY
sections.text:
Mother: History of episodic migraine headaches (managed conservatively).

Father: No significant medical history.

No family history of epilepsy, stroke, or intracranial pathology.

PERSONAL HISTORY

Occupation: Software engineer (desk-based; prolonged screen time)

Diet: Mixed vegetarian and non-vegetarian

Sleep: Approximately 5-6 hours per night (suboptimal)

Smoking: Non-smoker

Alcohol: Occasional (social, approximately 1-2 units per month)

Exercise: Minimal (sedentary lifestyle)

Caffeine: Moderate intake (2-3 cups of coffee per day)

CURRENT MEDICATION

Paracetamol 500 mg — oral — as needed (PRN) — self-medicated for headaches.

No prescription medications.

sections.heading: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
sections.text:

NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION

Speech fluent. No dysarthria or dysphasia.

sections.name: ASSESSMENT
sections.heading: ASSESSMENT
sections.text:
26-year-old male presenting with a four-month history of recurrent episodic

headaches with migrainous features (unilateral, throbbing, photophobia).

Neurological examination is unremarkable with no focal deficit. The clinical

presentation is most consistent with migraine without aura. However, given the

relatively recent onset and frequency of headaches, further investigation is
warranted to exclude secondary causes.

Differential Diagnosis:

1. Migraine without aura (primary headache) — most likely

2. Tension-type headache — less likely given unilateral and throbbing quality

3. Secondary causes (intracranial pathology} — low clinical suspicion but
investigation recommended given relatively recent onset

sections.name: INVESTIGATIONS
sections.heading: 1. INVESTIGATIONS
sections.text:
- MRI Brain (with and without contrast) — to exclude structural pathology
and secondary causes of headache.

- Routine blood work: CBC, ESR, CRP, Thyroid function (TSH).

2. CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT (pending MRI results):

- Sleep hygiene counselling: aim for 7-8 hours per night.

- Reduce prolonged screen exposure; take regular breaks (20-20-20 rule).

- Maintain a headache diary (record frequency, duration, triggers, severity).

- Adequate hydration.

- Limit caffeine to 1-2 cups per day.

3. ACUTE TREATMENT:

- Continue Paracetamol 500 mg PRN (max 2g/day) for acute episodes.

- If Paracetamol is insufficient, may use Ibuprofen 400 mg PRN (if no
contraindications). Advise against frequent analgesic use (>10 days/month)
to prevent medication-overuse headache.

sections.name: FOLLOW_UP
sections.heading: 4. FOLLOW-UP
sections.text:
- Review after MRI Brain with the imaging report.

- If headache frequency persists or worsens, consider preventive therapy
at next visit.

- Return sooner if: new neurological symptoms, sudden severe headache,
visual changes, seizures, or progressive worsening.
